question: On abdominal ultrasound, fatty liver (hepatic steatosis) characteristically appears as increased echogenicity of the liver parenchyma compared with the adjacent renal cortex, with posterior attenuation of the sound beam.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. The key ultrasound sign of fatty liver is hyperechogenicity of the liver relative to the renal cortex — a simple, quick comparison that requires no contrast or radiation. Posterior sound attenuation is an additional sign in moderate-to-severe steatosis.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The liver is normally isoechoic or minimally hyperechoic compared with the kidney. In fatty liver, intracellular fat deposition increases reflectivity, making the liver conspicuously brighter than the kidney (loss of normal liver–kidney echotexture), with progressive attenuation of the sound beam in severe steatosis. This is the quickest bedside USG sign.
